cls: Dietary supplement / herbal botanical (anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, choleretic; curcuminoid-containing)
pharm: Dried rhizome of Curcuma longa and its standardized extracts contain curcuminoids (chiefly curcumin) and a volatile oil; the curcuminoids are thought to modulate inflammatory signaling (e.g., NF-kB, COX, and LOX pathways) and to act as antioxidants, while the whole rhizome has traditional choleretic/carminative use for digestive complaints.
quick: Supplement: turmeric extract/curcumin commonly ~500-2000 mg/day in divided doses; EMA traditional-use dried rhizome powder for dyspepsia ~1.5-3 g/day
Take with food containing fat and/or with piperine (black pepper) to improve poor oral absorption
Avoid medicinal/high (supplement) doses; culinary spice amounts generally regarded as acceptable
Avoid medicinal/high doses; safety of supplement doses not established; culinary amounts likely acceptable
No established adjustment; data limited - use cautiously
Caution - rare reports of hepatotoxicity with high-dose extracts; avoid in active liver disease
No specific interaction documented; avoid combining hepatotoxic exposures
GI tolerability, bleeding signs (esp. with anticoagulants/surgery), liver enzymes if high-dose/prolonged use
summary: Curcuma longa (turmeric) is the rhizome of a plant in the ginger family, used widely as a culinary spice (GRAS) and as a dietary supplement; its principal active constituents are curcuminoids, chiefly curcumin. It is NOT an FDA-approved drug, and the information here is drawn from non-FDA authoritative herbal monograph sources (NIH NCCIH, the EMA HMPC herbal monograph for Curcumae longae rhizoma, and WHO/NMCD-type references). Traditional and supplement uses center on digestive complaints (dyspepsia) and on anti-inflammatory/antioxidant support. Curcumin has poor oral bioavailability and is often formulated with piperine or as enhanced-absorption preparations and taken with fatty food. It is generally well tolerated, with gastrointestinal upset the most common adverse effect at higher doses; rare reports of hepatotoxicity and allergic reactions exist. Because of antiplatelet potential and possible effects on drug metabolism, use caution with anticoagulants/antiplatelets, before surgery, and in biliary obstruction or gallstones (cholagogue effect).
indications: Traditional use for symptomatic relief of digestive complaints such as dyspepsia, bloating, and flatulence (EMA traditional herbal use for the dried rhizome)
Dietary supplement use for general anti-inflammatory and antioxidant support
Folk/traditional use as a cholagogue (to stimulate bile flow) for minor digestive disturbance
Commonly used as a culinary spice and food coloring (GRAS)

dosage.c: Dyspepsia / digestive complaints (traditional use - dried rhizome powder)
dosage.d: Approximately 1.5-3 g of dried rhizome powder per day in divided doses (per EMA HMPC traditional-use monograph)
dosage.n: Traditional herbal use; not a substantiated medical claim. Discontinue and seek advice if symptoms persist beyond 2 weeks

dosage.d: Commonly ~500-2000 mg/day of extract/curcumin in divided doses (product-dependent)
dosage.n: No single established therapeutic dose; follow product labeling. Poor bioavailability - often combined with piperine
Food-level intake is generally regarded as safe

admin: Take with a meal that contains some fat to improve absorption of poorly soluble curcuminoids
Co-administration with piperine (black pepper extract) substantially increases curcumin absorption; many supplements are formulated this way
Follow the dosing on the specific product label, as extract concentration and standardization vary widely between brands
Discontinue before planned surgery (commonly advised ~2 weeks beforehand) because of possible antiplatelet effect - confirm timing with the surgical team
Inform clinicians it is being taken, especially when on anticoagulant/antiplatelet drugs or medicines with a narrow therapeutic index
moa: The proposed activity of turmeric is attributed mainly to curcuminoids (especially curcumin). Curcumin is described in herbal and preclinical literature as having anti-inflammatory effects through downregulation of pro-inflammatory transcription factors such as nuclear factor-kappa B (NF-kB) and inhibition of inflammatory enzymes including cyclooxygenase (COX) and lipoxygenase (LOX), and as an antioxidant/free-radical scavenger. The whole rhizome also has a traditional choleretic/cholagogue action (stimulating bile secretion and flow) and carminative effect, which underpin its traditional use for dyspepsia. These mechanisms are largely proposed/preclinical and from traditional use rather than established by definitive clinical evidence.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity/allergy to turmeric, curcumin, or other Curcuma species
relative: Biliary obstruction, bile duct obstruction, or gallstones (cholagogue/choleretic effect may worsen - avoid medicinal doses)
Active bleeding, bleeding disorders, or concurrent anticoagulant/antiplatelet therapy (possible additive bleeding risk)
The 2 weeks before scheduled surgery (theoretical increased bleeding risk)
Pregnancy and lactation at medicinal/high doses (safety not established)
Active or significant liver disease (rare hepatotoxicity reports with high-dose extracts)
monitor: Signs of bleeding or bruising, particularly with anticoagulants/antiplatelets or perioperatively
Liver enzymes if used in high doses or for prolonged periods
Effect on co-administered narrow-therapeutic-index drugs (possible metabolism changes)

preg: Medicinal and high (supplement) doses should be avoided in pregnancy because safety has not been established and traditional sources raise theoretical concerns; turmeric used in normal culinary/spice amounts as part of food is generally regarded as acceptable. Discuss any supplement use with the obstetric provider.
lact: Safety of medicinal/high supplement doses during breastfeeding has not been established, so these should be avoided; turmeric consumed in culinary amounts as a food/spice is generally regarded as acceptable.
renal: No established dose adjustment for renal impairment; specific data are limited. Use cautiously and at usual food/supplement amounts, and discuss prolonged high-dose use with a clinician.
hepatic: Use with caution. Although turmeric is generally well tolerated, there are rare reports of hepatotoxicity associated with high-dose turmeric/curcumin supplements; avoid medicinal doses in active or significant liver disease and monitor for jaundice, dark urine, or right-upper-quadrant pain.

major: Anticoagulants and antiplatelet agents (e.g., warfarin, heparins, direct oral anticoagulants, aspirin, clopidogrel) - theoretical additive risk of bleeding from turmeric/curcumin antiplatelet effect
moderate: Drugs metabolized by CYP3A4 or transported by P-glycoprotein - possible alteration of drug levels (theoretical/limited evidence)
Piperine-containing products or supplements - increase curcumin absorption and may also raise levels of other co-administered drugs
Other herbs/supplements with antiplatelet or anticoagulant activity (e.g., ginkgo, garlic, ginger, fish oil) - additive bleeding risk
minor: Possible additive effect with antihyperglycemic agents (theoretical glucose-lowering)
Iron - high turmeric intake may bind dietary iron and theoretically reduce absorption
interactions.food: Best absorbed when taken with a fat-containing meal and/or with piperine (black pepper); curcumin is otherwise poorly absorbed.
interactions.alcohol: No specific documented interaction; avoid combining with other hepatotoxic exposures given rare reports of liver injury.
interactions.diagnostics: No well-characterized laboratory interference; high-dose use may rarely elevate liver enzymes.

serious: Hepatotoxicity / drug-induced liver injury (rare, reported with high-dose extracts)
Increased bleeding (theoretical, especially with anticoagulants/antiplatelets or surgery)
rare: Allergic/hypersensitivity reactions including contact dermatitis and rash
Worsening of gallbladder/biliary symptoms in those with gallstones or bile duct obstruction
emergency: Signs of severe allergic reaction (swelling, difficulty breathing, anaphylaxis)
Signs of liver injury (marked jaundice, dark urine, severe right-upper-quadrant pain)

monitoring: Gastrointestinal tolerability, particularly at higher supplement doses
Signs of bleeding or bruising in patients on anticoagulants/antiplatelets or around surgery
Liver enzymes and symptoms of liver injury if used in high doses or for prolonged periods
Resolution of dyspepsia within a reasonable period (seek medical advice if persistent beyond ~2 weeks)
Symptoms in patients with gallstones or biliary disease
counsel: This is a dietary supplement / herbal product, not an FDA-approved medicine; tell your healthcare provider you are taking it
Take it with a meal that has some fat, and products with black pepper (piperine) are absorbed better
Turmeric used in cooking as a spice is generally considered safe
Stop and tell your surgeon if you have an operation planned - it may increase bleeding; many advise stopping about 2 weeks before
If you take a blood thinner or antiplatelet medicine, check with your doctor before using turmeric supplements
Do not use medicinal doses if you have gallstones or blocked bile ducts, or if you are pregnant or breastfeeding, without medical advice
Stop and seek care if you develop yellowing of the skin/eyes, dark urine, severe stomach pain, or a rash with swelling or trouble breathing
If you are using it for indigestion and symptoms last more than about 2 weeks, see your healthcare provider
pk: Not well defined; for dyspepsia symptomatic effect may occur over days; supplement effects are not established clinically
Curcumin oral absorption is poor; measurable plasma levels are low and reached within a few hours when absorbed
Curcumin is rapidly metabolized (glucuronidation/sulfation) with a short systemic presence; specific human half-life poorly characterized
Short systemic exposure due to rapid metabolism and elimination; typically dosed once or twice daily
Store in a cool, dry place away from light and moisture; keep tightly closed per product labeling
pearls: Turmeric (Curcuma longa) is a dietary supplement / herbal, NOT an FDA-approved drug; the information here is from non-FDA authoritative herbal monograph sources (NIH NCCIH, EMA HMPC monograph for Curcumae longae rhizoma, WHO/NMCD-type references). It is GRAS as a food/spice

Curcumin has poor oral bioavailability - it is rapidly metabolized and poorly absorbed; piperine (black pepper) and fat-containing meals improve absorption, and many products are formulated for enhanced bioavailability
Possible antiplatelet effect: use caution with anticoagulants/antiplatelets and stop before surgery because of theoretical increased bleeding risk
Caution in gallstones or biliary obstruction - turmeric is a choleregic/cholagogue and may worsen symptoms
Generally well tolerated; high doses most often cause GI upset (nausea, diarrhea), and there are rare reports of hepatotoxicity and allergic reactions
May affect drug-metabolizing enzymes/transporters (CYP3A4, P-glycoprotein) in theory - be cautious with narrow-therapeutic-index medications
missed: There is no strict schedule for a supplement. If you miss a dose, you can take it when you remember, or simply skip it and take the next dose at your usual time. Do not take a double dose to make up for a missed one.
overdose: There is no specific antidote. Turmeric has a wide margin of safety as a food, and excessive supplement intake most commonly causes gastrointestinal upset (nausea, diarrhea, abdominal discomfort). Management is supportive, with attention to hydration. Seek medical care for signs of an allergic reaction, unusual bleeding, or symptoms suggesting liver injury (jaundice, dark urine, severe abdominal pain).
